items.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
items.tldr: A Russian Kh‑101 cruise missile and two other projectiles entered Polish airspace during a large‑scale Coalition of the Willing exercise, prompting Warsaw and NATO to label the incident a deliberate provocation. No casualties were reported, but the breach underscores the growing risk of spill‑over from Russia’s intensified air campaign against Ukraine.
items.background: On 21 November 2026, Russia launched one of its biggest aerial assaults on Ukraine since the 2022 invasion, striking Kyiv bridges and a Lviv railway station. Simultaneously, a UK‑ and France‑led drill named Koalicja 2026 was underway in southeastern Poland, involving 11 nations preparing for a potential peace‑keeping role. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the missile strike near the exercise area was "no coincidence," while Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak‑Kamysz called it a provocation and requested additional NATO support. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned the "grave violations" and confirmed allied jets were scrambled. The incident follows a similar missile landing in Poland in July 2026 and the 2022 fatal strike that killed two Polish farmers.

analysis.heading: Strategic Signaling by Moscow
analysis.content: The timing of the Kh‑101 incursion—coincident with a high‑visibility multinational exercise—suggests a calculated Russian effort to signal resolve and test NATO’s Article 5 thresholds without triggering a full‑scale response. By using a precision‑guided cruise missile that crashed harmlessly in a rural zone, Moscow can claim plausible deniability while still demonstrating the ability to penetrate NATO airspace at will. This mirrors the 2022 Przewodów incident, where a Ukrainian air‑defence missile fell in Poland, but the current event involves a Russian‑origin weapon, raising the political stakes.

analysis.heading: NATO Cohesion and Rapid Reaction
analysis.content: NATO’s immediate scrambling of jets and Rutte’s public condemnation illustrate the alliance’s commitment to collective defence and its readiness to act on airspace violations. The joint visit of five coalition defence ministers—including UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting—to the exercise site reinforces political unity and sends a deterrent message. However, the reliance on diplomatic language ("provocation," "unacceptable") rather than invoking Article 5 indicates a calibrated approach aimed at avoiding escalation while maintaining credibility.

analysis.heading: Impact on the Coalition of the Willing and Future Exercises
analysis.content: The Coalition of the Willing, a flexible grouping of Ukraine’s key supporters, is using Koalicja 2026 to rehearse interoperability for a potential post‑conflict stabilization mission. The missile strike forces the coalition to reassess force protection, air‑defence integration, and the political risk of conducting drills near the front line. It may accelerate the deployment of additional NATO air‑defence assets (e.g., Patriot batteries) to Poland and prompt a review of exercise locations farther from the Ukrainian border.

analysis.heading: Escalation Risks and Air‑Defence Posture
analysis.content: Repeated airspace breaches—Poland in July 2026, Moldova on the same day, and the 2022 fatal incident—create a pattern that could compel NATO to adopt a more robust forward‑based air‑defence architecture. The presence of Russian long‑range cruise missiles (Kh‑101, Kalibr) and jet‑powered drones (likely Geran‑2 variants) in the same salvo complicates interception, requiring layered defences (SHORAD, medium‑range, and electronic warfare). Any misidentification or delayed response could trigger a broader confrontation.

key_facts: A Russian Kh‑101 cruise missile struck near Nowy Lipowiec, ~50 km from the Ukrainian border, at 06:30 local time.
Two additional objects—a suspected missile near Rudnik nad Sanem and a jet‑powered drone near Mołodycz—also entered Polish airspace.
No injuries or material damage were reported; the impact was captured on a farm camera.
The incursion occurred during Koalicja 2026, an 11‑nation exercise led by the UK and France in southeastern Poland.
Polish PM Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak‑Kamysz labeled the event a deliberate provocation and requested extra NATO support.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned the violations and confirmed allied jets were scrambled.
Moldova reported a separate drone airspace violation on the same day, its 118th since February 2022.
implications: NATO may accelerate deployment of additional air‑defence systems to Poland and the Baltic states.
The Coalition of the Willing will likely revise exercise security protocols and consider relocating drills further west.
Russia’s use of precision missiles for signalling could lower the threshold for future kinetic demonstrations against NATO territory.
Increased political pressure on Moscow to clarify its rules of engagement, potentially leading to diplomatic talks on de‑confliction mechanisms.
items.outlook: In the near term, expect heightened NATO air‑patrol activity over eastern Poland and a formal request to the NATO‑Russia Council for a de‑confliction dialogue. The Coalition of the Willing will likely issue a joint statement reaffirming commitment to Ukraine while announcing enhanced force‑protection measures for upcoming exercises. If Russia repeats such incursions, the alliance may move from declaratory condemnation to concrete reinforcement—potentially invoking Article 4 consultations and positioning additional Patriot or IRIS‑T batteries on Polish soil. The incident also adds urgency to EU‑level discussions on a unified air‑defence procurement strategy.

items.fulltext:
Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
- Published
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near MoÅodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa DÄba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

items.title: Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
items.tldr: Russia launched one of its largest aerial assaults of the war, striking three major bridges in Kyiv and railway infrastructure in Lviv, killing at least nine people. The attack came days after Ukraine severely damaged the Crimean Bridge, a key Russian supply artery, and coincided with diplomatic talks in Berlin where European leaders and U.S. envoys discussed security guarantees for Ukraine — proposals the Kremlin immediately rejected as unacceptable.
items.background: Since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Crimean Bridge has served as a critical logistical link for Russian forces in occupied southern Ukraine. Ukraine's successful operation to collapse a section of the bridge's roadway earlier this week represented both a tactical disruption and a symbolic blow to President Vladimir Putin, who personally inaugurated the bridge in 2019. In response, Putin vowed retaliation that would be "far more painful." The overnight barrage — involving over 110 missiles and 400 drones launched in staggered waves — targeted not only Kyiv's river crossings but also energy facilities and residential areas across multiple Ukrainian regions. Simultaneously, a meeting of the "coalition of the willing" in Berlin brought together European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, alongside U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, to discuss a potential peace framework. The Kremlin's deputy foreign minister, Sergei Ryabkov, dismissed the idea of NATO Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine as "unacceptable," reiterating Russia's long-standing opposition to any NATO alignment for Kyiv.

analysis.heading: Escalation Dynamics and Retaliation Calculus
analysis.content: The scale and precision of Russia's latest strike — over 110 ballistic and cruise missiles combined with more than 400 attack drones launched in 20–30 minute intervals — signals a deliberate escalation designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses and maximize civilian disruption. By targeting the Podilsko-Voskresensky, Darnytskyi, and Southern bridges in Kyiv, Russia aims to sever critical transport arteries linking the capital's left and right banks, complicating both civilian evacuation and military logistics. The simultaneous strike on Lviv's Sknyliv railway station, a primary entry point for international aid and personnel, extends the pressure to western Ukraine, previously less affected by heavy bombardment. This pattern mirrors Russia's 2022–2023 winter campaign against energy infrastructure but with a sharper focus on transportation nodes, suggesting an evolving doctrine of strategic interdiction.

analysis.heading: Diplomatic Crosscurrents and Security Guarantee Debates
analysis.content: The Berlin meeting highlighted deepening fractures between Western allies and Russia over the architecture of any future settlement. Jared Kushner's assertion that Russia is "comfortable" with NATO Article 5-based guarantees contradicts Sergei Ryabkov's categorical rejection of "quasi-NATO" membership, exposing a fundamental disconnect in how each side defines security assurances. Meanwhile, President Trump's reported skepticism about the €70 billion European military aid package — voiced en route from a summit with Xi Jinping in China — introduces uncertainty about U.S. commitment levels. The presence of both U.S. and European envoys at the same table, yet with divergent messaging, risks creating diplomatic ambiguity that Moscow could exploit to delay negotiations while consolidating battlefield gains.

analysis.heading: Infrastructure Targeting and Civilian Impact
analysis.content: The closure of all three major Kyiv bridges and the damage to Lviv's railway hub illustrate a shift toward systematic degradation of Ukraine's national mobility. Mayor Vitali Klitschko's warning against non-essential travel into the capital underscores the immediate humanitarian and economic consequences: disrupted supply chains, hindered emergency services, and psychological strain on a population already enduring near-nightly air raid sirens. The reported damage to the Austrian and Dutch embassies adds a diplomatic dimension, potentially invoking Vienna Convention protections and drawing further international condemnation. France's call for a UN Security Council meeting, while symbolically important, faces likely Russian veto, limiting practical outcomes.

analysis.heading: NATO and European Response Coordination
analysis.content: The Polish report of a Russian cruise missile landing 50km from its border — the second such incident in weeks — triggered NATO scrambling of Polish and Swedish jets, demonstrating the alliance's heightened readiness on its eastern flank. The joint UK-French leadership of Exercise Koalicja, involving 11 nations and thousands of troops in Poland, signals a concrete move toward operationalizing the "coalition of the willing" concept beyond political declarations. However, Donald Tusk's characterization of the missile strike as "intentional provocation" raises the threshold for Article 4 consultations, testing NATO's collective resolve without crossing into direct conflict. The alliance's ability to calibrate deterrence while avoiding escalation will be a defining challenge in the coming months.

key_facts: Russia launched over 110 missiles and 400+ drones in a nationwide overnight assault, killing at least 9 (7 in Kyiv, 2 in Lviv) and injuring 28+.
Three major Kyiv bridges — Podilsko-Voskresensky, Darnytskyi, and Southern — were struck and closed, severing key Dnipro River crossings.
Ukraine's prior operation collapsed a road section of the Crimean Bridge, a vital Russian supply line to occupied Crimea and southern front lines.
Kremlin deputy FM Sergei Ryabkov rejected NATO Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine as "unacceptable," contradicting U.S. envoy claims.
A Russian cruise missile landed in Poland, 50km from the Ukrainian border, prompting NATO jet scrambles and Polish accusations of "intentional provocation."
implications: Russia's demonstrated capacity for sustained, high-volume precision strikes against hardened infrastructure suggests a replenished missile/drone stockpile, likely aided by domestic production and Iranian/North Korean transfers, prolonging its ability to wage attritional warfare.

The diplomatic deadlock over security guarantees — with Russia insisting on neutrality and the West exploring NATO-linked frameworks — makes a negotiated settlement unlikely before one side achieves a decisive battlefield shift or exhaustion.

Repeated Russian missile incursions into NATO airspace (Poland) normalize brinkmanship, increasing the risk of miscalculation that could trigger Article 4 or 5 consultations, especially as European forces conduct large-scale exercises nearby.

Ukraine's reliance on western logistics hubs like Lviv makes them high-value targets; sustained degradation could impede allied military aid delivery and civilian evacuation, weakening Kyiv's strategic depth.
items.outlook: Expect Russia to maintain high-intensity strikes on transport and energy infrastructure through winter, leveraging improved drone swarm tactics to saturate defenses. Diplomatic tracks will remain paralyzed as long as Moscow rejects any NATO nexus for Ukraine and Washington sends mixed signals on aid. NATO's eastern flank exercises will expand, but the alliance will avoid direct intervention unless a clear Article 5 threshold is crossed. Ukraine's counteroffensive capacity depends on sustained Western munitions flow — now more vulnerable to interdiction at western entry points. The Crimean Bridge's partial destruction will force Russian logistics rerouting through the Kerch Strait ferry and land corridor, creating new choke points for Ukrainian targeting.

items.fulltext:
Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
- Published
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".
The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.
At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.
The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.
The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit â¬70bn (Â£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.
The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.
On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country.
It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.
Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.
Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.
France's foreign minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.
He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

items.title: French Court Convicts Police in Zecler Beating, Upholds Racist Aggravation
items.tldr: A French court convicted three police officers for the 2020 beating of Black music producer Michel Zecler and for falsifying a police report, accepting racism as an aggravating circumstance. The verdict, built on CCTV evidence and Zecler’s testimony, imposes prison terms and lifetime bans from policing, intensifying debate over systemic racism and excessive force in French policing.
items.background: In November 2020, during France’s Covid lockdown, Michel Zecler was stopped near his Paris recording studio for not wearing a mask. Officers followed him inside without a warrant, tried to remove him, and beat him. CCTV footage showed Zecler suffering some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance. The officers claimed he had violently resisted arrest and filed a falsified police report. The case became a cause célèbre for critics of French policing. The two-week trial was heard by a panel of five judges. The court accepted Zecler’s testimony that officers used a racial slur during the beating, finding racism to be an aggravating circumstance. Aurelien Lapersonne, Philippe Tondeux and Pierre Plantier each received five-year sentences with differing suspended portions; Plantier will serve one year under an ankle monitor. All were banned from police service.

analysis.heading: Legal Accountability and the Weight of CCTV
analysis.content: The verdict is legally significant because the court treated racism as an aggravating circumstance, toughening the sentences. That finding rested heavily on Zecler’s credibility: the judges noted that, unlike the officers, his account was verifiable in its details. The falsified police report was equally damaging. It transformed the case from a disputed use-of-force incident into a test of police honesty, and CCTV became the decisive counter-witness. The outcome signals that French courts can impose meaningful consequences for both violence and cover-up, though the suspended portions of the sentences mean only one officer will be immediately detained. The lifetime bans from policing are a strong symbolic and professional sanction. The ruling may become a reference point for how racism aggravators are argued in future cases involving police conduct, especially where video evidence exists.

analysis.heading: Policing, Race and Public Trust in France
analysis.content: The case has long been cited by critics as evidence of systemic racism and impunity within French policing. The officers admitted the beating and the fake report but denied racial motivation; the court’s rejection of that denial is central to the verdict’s social meaning. For many communities, the ruling validates longstanding complaints that racial bias affects how police stop, arrest and use force against Black men. At the same time, police unions and officers may argue that the case has become a symbol used to stigmatise the force. The verdict arrives amid renewed criticism of alleged excessive force at recent protests, making the question of public trust especially acute. Reform advocates are likely to point to the need for stronger independent oversight, better warrant compliance, body-worn cameras and anti-bias training. Institutional resistance to such changes remains substantial, but the court’s findings make the status quo harder to defend.

analysis.heading: Political and Social Reverberations
analysis.content: The verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler’s supporters and is likely to reverberate beyond the courtroom. Because the case became a cause célèbre during the 2020 racial-justice protests, it connects French debates over policing to wider global conversations about race, accountability and state violence. The French government faces a familiar balancing act: maintaining public order and police morale while responding to demands for civil-liberties protections and minority rights. The officers’ apologies in court may soften some public anger, but they do not resolve the underlying policy questions. The case also has an industry dimension: media coverage, legal analysis and civil-society monitoring have turned the trial into a public referendum on police transparency. Expect further debate over how CCTV and other evidence are preserved, how complaints against officers are investigated, and whether racism aggravators are applied consistently.

key_facts: Three French police officers were convicted over the 2020 beating of Black music producer Michel Zecler in Paris.
The court upheld racism as an aggravating circumstance, finding that officers used a racial slur during the beating.
The officers were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report claiming Zecler violently resisted arrest.
CCTV footage showed Zecler receiving some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance.
Aurelien Lapersonne, Philippe Tondeux and Pierre Plantier received five-year sentences with differing suspended portions; all were banned from policing.
The incident began during Covid lockdown when officers stopped Zecler for not wearing a mask and followed him into his studio without a warrant.
implications: The ruling strengthens the legal precedent for treating racism as an aggravating factor in French police misconduct cases.
It deepens scrutiny of police credibility when official reports conflict with video evidence.
The case will intensify pressure for independent police oversight and reform of stop-and-search and use-of-force practices.
Police unions may warn of demoralisation, while civil-rights groups will cite the verdict as proof that accountability is possible.
items.outlook: The verdict is unlikely to end France’s policing debate. Appeals or further legal challenges may follow, but the court’s factual findings will remain politically potent. Zecler’s case is now a reference point for arguments about systemic racism, video accountability and the limits of police discretion. The French government will face continued pressure to strengthen oversight mechanisms while avoiding a rupture with police ranks. Public attention will next focus on how the sentences are served, whether the officers appeal, and whether the ruling influences pending cases involving protest policing and alleged excessive force.

items.fulltext:
French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
- Published
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".
